s: E. Unprotected and less-protected categories.
Historically unprotected categories are "well-defined and narrowly limited" (Chaplinsky v. New Hampshire, 1942).
Courts may not create new ones by balancing (Stevens; Brown v. Entertainment Merchants, 2011, violent video games; United States v. Alvarez, 2012, lies about military medals).
Even within a category, viewpoint discrimination is forbidden (R.A.V. v. St. Paul, 1992).
Categories and their tests.
Incitement (Brandenburg v. Ohio, 1969): advocacy directed to inciting imminent lawless action and likely to produce it.
True threats (Virginia v. Black, 2003; Counterman v. Colorado, 2023): serious expressions of intent to commit unlawful violence against particular people.
The speaker must at least have acted recklessly as to the threatening character.
Fighting words (Chaplinsky): face-to-face personal insults likely to provoke immediate violence.
Narrowly construed today.
Obscenity (Miller v. California, 1973):
appeals to the prurient interest under contemporary community standards;
depicts sexual conduct in a patently offensive way as defined by state law;
taken as a whole, lacks serious literary, artistic, political or scientific value (judged by a national reasonable-person standard).
Child pornography is unprotected without regard to Miller (New York v. Ferber, 1982), but virtual images are protected (Ashcroft v. Free Speech Coalition, 2002).
Age-verification requirements for sexual content harmful to minors receive intermediate scrutiny (Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton, 2025).
Defamation:
Public officials and public figures must prove actual malice: knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard (New York Times v. Sullivan, 1964; Curtis Publishing v. Butts, 1967).
Private figures need show only fault (at least negligence) for actual damages, and actual malice for presumed or punitive damages (Gertz v. Robert Welch, 1974).
For private figures on matters of private concern, the protections relax (Dun & Bradstreet, 1985).
Intentional infliction of emotional distress claims by public figures require actual malice (Hustler v. Falwell, 1988).
Speech on public matters at a funeral is protected (Snyder v. Phelps, 2011).
Commercial speech (Central Hudson, 1980):
Is the speech about lawful activity and not misleading?
(If not, it is unprotected.)
Is the government interest substantial?
Does the regulation directly advance that interest?
Is it not more extensive than necessary (a reasonable fit)?
Content- and speaker-based burdens may get heightened review (Sorrell v. IMS Health, 2011).
